analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the federal estate tax, which applies to large inheritances left at death, along with the gift tax on large transfers between living people and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. The estate tax in 2012 applied only to estates worth more than about $5 million, so the money saved would go almost entirely to the heirs of the very largest estates. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than the roughly $5 million exemption, and people planning to give large gifts while alive, would owe less or nothing in tax. The benefit is concentrated at the very top: only a small fraction of estates are large enough to owe any estate tax at all.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, applying to deaths, gifts, and transfers after enactment [S2] [S3].
Because the estate tax in 2012 exempted roughly the first $5 million of an estate, repeal would deliver its savings almost entirely to heirs of the wealthiest families.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose the revenue those taxes raise, a burden that falls on everyone else through more borrowing or higher taxes elsewhere. Repeal would also remove a tax that falls only on very large inheritances, shifting more of the overall tax load onto earnings from work.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would eliminate the federal taxes that apply only to the largest fortunes, shrinking federal revenue and increasing borrowing or the tax burden on other sources [S2] [S3].
The repeal would apply after enactment, cutting the tax immediately for deaths and gifts occurring afterward with no phase-in [S3].

Supporters of repeal argue the estate tax taxes assets that were already taxed once when earned, and that it can force heirs of farms and small businesses to sell assets to pay the bill; the bill addressed this by full repeal rather than raising the exemption or adding protections for small estates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would flow to a small group of very wealthy families, while the cost is spread across every taxpayer through lost revenue. It did not pair repeal with any replacement revenue, so its net effect would be a large, permanent tax cut for the heirs of the largest estates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Boozman introduced the bill on July 19, 2012, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S5] [S1].
The action history shows no further activity after the committee referral, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the estate tax continued to apply to the largest estates, and the federal revenue it raises was preserved rather than eliminated. Everyday taxpayers are better off than they would have been under repeal, since the cost of repeal would have been spread to them through borrowing or other taxes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who keep the estate tax revenue

for.name: Sen. John Boozman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act and it was referred to the Finance Committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Repeal would permanently eliminate the estate tax on inheritances above the roughly $5 million exemption, a direct gain for the largest estates. The lost revenue would be made up by everyone else through borrowing or other taxes.
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would disappear with no replacement revenue, meaning more federal debt or higher taxes from other sources for ordinary earners.
